title: Pediatric neurobrucellosis and atypical Guillain-Barré syndrome: an intriguing case unveiled
case_prompt:
A previously healthy 5-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of progressive walking difficulty. She first noted heaviness and pain in her lower limbs, then developed asymmetric weakness beginning in the right leg and subsequently involving the left, leading to loss of ambulation over four weeks. She denied sensory changes in the upper limbs or sphincter problems. Two weeks before onset of her gait difficulties, she had high-grade fever, sweating, chills, myalgia, and neck and back pain but no respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms. She had consumed raw camel milk before fever onset. 

On examination, temperature was 38.1 °C; other vital signs were stable. She was lethargic, with positive Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs. Cranial nerves and cognition were intact. Muscle bulk and tone were normal. Strength was 4/5 in bilateral hip flexion, 3/5 in right knee flexion, 4/5 in left knee flexion, 4/5 in right ankle dorsiflexion, and normal elsewhere in the lower limbs; upper-limb strength was normal. Deep tendon reflexes were diminished in all limbs. Sensation and cerebellar testing were normal. Gait was wide based; Romberg sign was negative. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests revealed normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function, thyroid studies, and serum creatine kinase (37 U/L). ESR was 18 mm/h. ANA and anti–double-stranded DNA were negative. Blood cultures showed no growth. Serum Brucella antibody titer was 1:1280 positive for both Brucella melitensis and Brucella abortus. Lumbar puncture showed 0 cells, protein 1545 mg/dL, and glucose 3.34 mmol/L; CSF cultures were negative. MRI of the lumbosacral spine with contrast showed enhancement of the spinal meninges and thickened cauda equina nerve roots. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated a mixed axonal and demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Metabolic disorders were considered — “Examples of metabolic disorders are diabetes, porphyria, and vitamin deficiencies.” [patient’s vitamin D level was normal]  
2. Guillain–Barré syndrome was considered — “Given the progression of her symptoms after her initial flu-like symptoms, GBS was highly suspected.” [lack of facial, upper limb, or respiratory involvement made typical GBS less likely]  
3. Neurosarcoidosis was considered — “Inflammatory conditions may include GBS, neurosarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Sjögren's syndrome.”  
4. Systemic lupus erythematosus was considered — “Inflammatory conditions may include GBS, neurosarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Sjögren's syndrome.” [ANA and double-stranded DNA tests came back negative]  
5. Sjögren's syndrome was considered — “Inflammatory conditions may include GBS, neurosarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Sjögren's syndrome.”  
6. Cryptococcal infection was considered — “Infectious causes may involve fungal or bacterial etiologies such as cryptococcal infection, tuberculosis, or brucellosis.”  
7. Tuberculosis was considered — “Infectious causes may involve fungal or bacterial etiologies such as cryptococcal infection, tuberculosis, or brucellosis.”  
8. Brucellosis was considered — “The serum Brucella antibody titer was elevated at 1:1280, positive for both Brucella melitensis and Brucella abortus.”  
9. Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis was considered — “Examples of neoplastic processes are leptomeningeal carcinomatosis and lymphoma.”  
10. Lymphoma was considered — “Examples of neoplastic processes are leptomeningeal carcinomatosis and lymphoma.”
